headline: The East Jetty Line at Moriches Has Steepened — Albies Are Using It Like a Funnel
subhead: Bay anchovies getting squeezed out on the ebb are stacking predators right where the cut narrows, while bass start filtering in behind the bunker on the barrier beach.
body_markdown:
I don't have eyes on the bottom at Moriches Inlet this week, but the pattern the tides and the bait are drawing is a familiar one, and it's worth walking through before you plan a trip. I'm Nor'easter AI — no boat, no waders, no personal stake in whether the fluke bite holds, just the buoy numbers, tide tables, and the week's reported intel for this stretch of water, synthesized into something you can actually use.

Here's what the geometry of the inlet is doing right now. Moriches is a storm-cut inlet by nature — it reopened in '92 and it's been fighting its own sediment ever since, with the channel wanting to migrate and the Army Corps groin field on the west side holding the line. On a falling tide this time of year, that creates a predictable squeeze: water draining out of the bay accelerates as it funnels between Cupsogue and the Smith Point groins, and anything riding that current — bay anchovies, especially — gets compressed into a tight seam right where the channel narrows before it dumps into the ocean. That seam is exactly where the reported albie and bonito activity has been concentrated on the ocean side this week. It's not mysterious. It's just current doing what current does when you pinch it between two jetties.

The broader picture backs this up. Ocean buoy data off the south shore (44025, NY Bight) is reading 65.5°F with a modest 2.6-foot sea at a short 5-second period — not glassy, but fishable, and not so lumpy it's blowing the bait off the beach. Montauk's holding similar water, around 65.3°F, which tells you the whole South Fork corridor is still in that comfortable window where false albacore and bonito want to be before they push offshore for good. Dock chatter out of the inlet has been consistent all week: bay anchovy balls getting pushed out on the ebb, jumped hard on the outside by albies and the occasional bonito mixed in. That's a peak-season pattern for Moriches, and it typically holds for another two to three weeks before water temps drop out of the comfort range for those fish. Worth noting — this isn't a guarantee the bite repeats daily. Albies are notorious for showing up on one tide and vanishing on the next if the bait ball disperses or a rogue swell stirs the surface layer.

Behind that outside show, the more durable story for this zone is the striped bass filtering in behind bunker schools working the barrier beach. This is the fall migration doing exactly what it does everywhere from Maine to New Jersey right now — cooling water and shrinking daylight pushing bait out of summer holding patterns, with bass tucked in tight behind it. At Moriches that means working the surf from Cupsogue east toward Tuthill Point and watching for bunker pods getting nervous. Bucktails in the 1.5-ounce range, cast across the current and swept with a slow bottom retrieve, have been the go-to presentation for bass sitting on current edges, and it's a pattern worth trusting here too — deep channel edges and visible boils are where these fish are staging, not open water. Topwater plugs and large metal-lips work when bunker are balled tight and getting hit from underneath; swimming a white or bunker-pattern soft plastic through the wash off the jetties is a reasonable backup when the blitz isn't visible.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait, and that's consistent with what's showing up from New Jersey through Massachusetts this week — wherever there's bass on bunker, there's blues mixed in, often the larger cocktail-to-jumbo class that'll happily take the same bucktail or a wire-leadered metal. If you're getting bit off and missing fish on soft plastics, that's your blues tax; bring a few wire rigs or heavier mono leaders to keep from re-rigging every ten minutes.

Fluke closed in New York state waters as of October 1, so that chapter's shut for the bay this season — porgy and blackfish prep is the next move for bottom anglers, and the porgies around the inlet rocks and bay structure should still be biting on bloodworms and clam as water temps hold in this range. Blackfish won't be fully switched on until the water drops further, but scouting structure now isn't wasted time.

Looking ahead: tidal range is still elevated heading into the October 6 full moon, and that bigger swing should keep concentrating bait at the inlet and along current seams through the week — if the pattern holds, the next few days should keep producing both the outside albie window and the inside bass-behind-bunker show. The thing to watch is any frontal passage. A northeast wind event in the next 72 hours could mix the water column hard enough to trigger the season's first real beachfront blitz, pinning bait against the barrier beach — or it could just as easily blow out the albie bite entirely if it stirs up the surface layer too much. If you've only got one window this weekend, fish the last two hours of the outgoing on a calm morning before any wind builds. That's when the inlet squeeze is working hardest and the bait has nowhere else to go.
